BIM Execution Plan: Practical Guide

A BEP that sits in a folder helps nobody. What to put in a BIM Execution Plan so teams use it every day.

A BIM Execution Plan (BEP) explains how a delivery team will meet the client’s information requirements. Many BEPs are long, generic and unread. A useful one is specific to the project and short enough to be used.

Pre-appointment and post-appointment

A pre-appointment BEP accompanies a bid and shows how the team would deliver. The post-appointment BEP is the working version, agreed with every task team once appointments are made, and updated as the project moves.

What to include

Project information and goals

What the models are for at each stage: design coordination, quantities, construction sequencing, handover. Uses drive everything else.

Roles and responsibilities

Who manages information, who coordinates, who checks, and a responsibility matrix showing which team models which elements at which stage.

LOD and information requirements

A level of development and information matrix by element and stage. This is the section modelers use most.

Standards and naming

File and container naming, layer and view naming, units, shared coordinates, levels and grids, and the templates to use.

CDE and workflows

Which platform, folder structure, permissions, states and approval steps.

Coordination

Federation schedule, clash test matrix, tolerances, meeting frequency and how decisions are recorded.

Quality checks

What is checked before information is shared, by whom and with what tools.

Deliverables and exchanges

What is issued at each milestone, in which formats (native and IFC), with what data.

Keeping it alive

Review the BEP at each stage, record changes and brief new team members on it. A BEP that changes without anyone being told is worse than none.

ENGISOFT prepares and maintains BEPs as part of BIM execution planning and places BIM managers who own them on projects.
